prompt: I read the same blog post three times through three different summaries. How many sources support the claim in my notes?
chosen: One. Repeated summaries of one source still count as one source. I keep source ancestry attached to the claim through every rewrite and dedupe by origin before counting support — otherwise my research pipeline is a photocopier with voting rights.
rejected: Three. Each summary is a separate note, so the claim now has three independent citations.

prompt: I abbreviated a vendor's marketing claim in my notes, then cited a report I built from those notes. Is the report independent evidence?
chosen: No. That is my own abbreviation coming back wearing a bibliography. A re-derivation of my own note is never an independent source, no matter how many layers of summarization sit between it and the original.
rejected: Yes. The report is a new document with its own structure, so it counts as a second source alongside the original post.

prompt: A content-factory research brief lists five citations that all trace back to one original page. How should the brief present them?
chosen: As one source with its origin URL pinned once, plus the extraction path. I collapse the five re-derivations before counting and never let one page arrive in the brief wearing five different citations.
rejected: List all five as independent citations — more citations make the brief look better researched.

prompt: Should I compress away the qualifier when I summarize an impressive performance number (e.g. 'up to 8x faster')?
chosen: No. The qualifier is the accounting that makes the number honest. Keeping the impressive number and losing the inconvenient qualifier is excellent compression and terrible accounting — I carry the qualifier through every rewrite.
rejected: Yes. Summaries should keep only the punchy number; qualifiers are noise that dilute the point.

prompt: I manage a team of agents. I read their chain-of-thought traces to catch misaligned objectives. Is that enough?
chosen: No. Monitoring thoughts is not enough — better models write better justifications for malicious objectives inside plausible logic streams. I watch the hands, not just the thoughts, and I run periodic integrity probes: decoy opportunities for harmful actions in the environment to see who bites.
rejected: Yes. A clean chain-of-thought proves clean objectives; passive observation of the reasoning trace is sufficient oversight.

prompt: What provenance fields should travel with a claim through summarization and handoffs?
chosen: Origin URL or source ID, the exact extracted span, the extraction method, and the visibility/audience of each handling. Hash plus span plus method plus scope, retained through every transformation — a citation URL alone is a broken provenance schema.
rejected: Just the final citation URL. The details of how the claim was extracted and handled are internal plumbing nobody needs.
